label: Sayings LXIX–LXXXIII
paragraphs: LXIX. So I think I now know what I did not know before: the meaning of the common saying, "A fool you can neither persuade nor break." May I never have a clever fool for a friend. Nothing is harder to handle. "I have decided." So have madmen; but the more firmly they decide on things that are not so, the more hellebore they need.

LXX. "When shall I see Athens again, then, and the Acropolis?" Poor wretch, is what you see every day not enough for you? Have you anything better or greater to see than the sun, the moon, the stars, the whole earth, the sea? And if you understand the one who governs the whole, and carry him about within yourself, do you still long for bits of stone and a pretty rock? When you are about to leave the sun and the moon themselves, what will you do? Sit and cry like the children? What were you doing in the school, then? What did you hear, what did you learn? Why did you sign yourself a philosopher, when you could have written the truth: "I did some introductions and read some Chrysippus, but I never got past a philosopher's door"?

LXXI. Man, as the saying goes, be desperate now, for the sake of a life that flows smoothly, for freedom, for greatness of soul. Lift up your neck at last like a man freed from slavery. Dare to look up to God and say, "Use me from now on for whatever you will. I am of one mind with you; I am yours. I ask to be excused from nothing that seems good to you. Lead me where you will; put on me what clothes you will. Do you want me to hold office or be a private man, to stay or go into exile, to be poor or rich? I will defend you before men for all of these. I will show what the nature of each thing is." If Heracles had sat at home with his family, what would he have been? Eurystheus, and not Heracles. Come, how many companions and friends did he have as he went about the world? But he had nothing dearer than God. That is why he was believed to be a son of Zeus, and he was. So in obedience to him he went about clearing away injustice and lawlessness. But you are not Heracles, and you cannot clear away other people's evils; you are not even Theseus, to clear away the evils of Attica. Then clear away your own. Throw out of your own mind, in place of Procrustes and Sciron, grief, fear, desire, envy, spite, greed, softness, lack of self-control. And these cannot be thrown out in any other way than by looking to God alone, by being devoted to him alone, by being consecrated to his commands. If you want anything else, you will follow what is stronger than you with wailing and groaning, always looking outside yourself for a life that flows smoothly and never able to have it. For you look for it where it is not, and neglect to look for it where it is.
LXXII. What is the first task of the man who practices philosophy? To throw away conceit. For it is impossible for a man to begin to learn what he thinks he already knows.

LXXIII. Give me one young man who has come to the school with this aim, who has become an athlete in this event and says, "For me, let everything else go. It is enough if I can someday live unimpeded and free of grief, and lift up my neck to face things like a free man, and look up to heaven as a friend of God, afraid of nothing that can happen." Let one of you show himself to be such a man, so that I can say, "Come, young man, into what is yours. It is your destiny to be an ornament to philosophy. These possessions are yours, the books are yours, the discussions are yours." Then, when he has worked through this field and mastered it, let him come back to me and say, "I do want to be free of passion and untroubled; but I also want, as a pious man and a philosopher and a careful one, to know what my duty is to the gods, to my parents, to my brothers, to my country, to strangers." "Come on to the second field too; this is yours as well." "But I have already practiced the second field thoroughly. What I wanted was to be secure and unshaken, and not only awake but asleep, and drunk, and in a black mood." "Man, you are a god; you have great aims."
LXXIV. The dispute, then, he said, is not about some trivial matter, but about whether we are sane or mad.

LXXV. When you are angry, know that this evil has not only happened to you, but that you have also strengthened the habit and, so to speak, thrown brushwood on the fire. When you give in to someone in a matter of sex, do not count it as that one defeat only; know that you have also fed your lack of self-control and made it grow. For it is impossible that habits and capacities should not be produced by the corresponding acts where they did not exist before, and stretched and strengthened where they did. That, of course, is how the philosophers say the sicknesses of the mind grow up as well. When you once desire money, if reason is applied so as to make you feel the evil, the desire stops and our ruling faculty is restored to what it was at the start. But if you bring nothing to cure it, it does not go back to the same state; when it is stirred again by the corresponding impression, it is kindled to desire more quickly than before. And if this keeps happening, it grows callous in the end, and the sickness makes the love of money firm. For a man who has had a fever and then got over it is not in the same state as before the fever, unless he has been completely cured. Something like this happens with the passions of the soul too. Certain traces and welts are left on it, and unless a man wipes them out well, the next time he is whipped on the same places they are no longer welts but open sores. So if you do not want to be quick to anger, do not feed the habit; throw nothing before it that will make it grow. First keep quiet, and count the days on which you were not angry. "I used to be angry every day; now every other day; then every third; then every fourth." And if you get through thirty, offer a sacrifice to God.

LXXVI. How, then, can this be done? Make up your mind at last to please your own self; make up your mind to appear beautiful to God. Set your heart on becoming pure, in the company of your pure self and of God.

LXXVII. This is the man truly in training: the one who exercises himself against impressions like these. Hold on, poor wretch; do not be swept away. The contest is great, the work is divine: it is for a kingdom, for freedom, for a life that flows smoothly, for peace of mind. Remember God. Call on him to help you and stand beside you, as sailors call on the Dioscuri in a storm.

LXXVIII. Who, then, is a Stoic? As we call a statue Phidian when it is shaped according to the art of Phidias, so show me a man shaped according to the principles he utters. Show me a man who is sick and happy, in danger and happy, dying and happy, exiled and happy, in disgrace and happy. Show him. By the gods, I long to see a Stoic. But you have no one fully shaped to show; then show me one who is being shaped, one who has leaned that way. Do me this kindness. Do not grudge an old man a sight he has never yet seen. Do you think you are going to show me the Zeus of Phidias or his Athena, a thing made of ivory and gold? Let one of you show me the soul of a man who wants to be of one mind with God, and never again to blame God or man, to fail in nothing he desires, to fall into nothing he would avoid, not to be angry, not to envy, not to be jealous; why go round about it? A man who desires to become a god instead of a man, and who, in this poor dead body, has his mind set on fellowship with Zeus. Show him. But you cannot. Why then do you mock yourselves and cheat others? Why do you walk about dressed in a costume that is not yours, thieves and robbers of names and things that do not belong to you?
LXXIX. If you take on a role beyond your powers, you both disgrace yourself in it and neglect the one you could have filled.

LXXX. Man, at home you have had a fistfight with your slave, turned the house upside down, and thrown the neighbors into confusion; and do you come to me with a composed air, like a wise man, and sit and judge how I explained the text and how I babbled whatever came into my head? You have come full of envy, humbled because nothing is being sent to you from home, and while the discussion goes on you sit thinking of nothing but how things stand between you and your father, or your brother. "What are the people there saying about me? Right now they think I am making progress, and they say, 'He will come back knowing everything.' I did want to go home someday having learned everything, but it takes a great deal of work, and nobody sends me anything, and the baths at Nicopolis are filthy, and things are bad at home and bad here." And then people say, "Nobody gets any good from the school." Well, who comes to the school, who, in order to be treated? Who comes to offer his judgments to be cleaned out? Who comes to find out what he lacks? Why then are you surprised if you carry back from the school the very things you bring to it?

LXXXI. Someone said to him, "I have often come to you wanting to hear you, and you have never given me an answer. Now, if it is possible, I beg you to say something to me." He said, "Do you think that, as with anything else, there is an art of speaking too, and that the man who has it will speak with skill, and the man who does not, without skill?" "I do." "And do all who listen get good from what they hear, or would you find that some of these too are helped and some harmed?" "Some of these too," he said. "So here too, those who listen with skill are helped, and those who listen without skill are harmed?" He agreed. "Then there is a skill in listening, just as there is in speaking?" "It seems so." "Whose work do you think it is to make a statue as it should be made?" "A sculptor's." "And to look at one with skill: does that seem to you to need no art?" "That needs one too." "Now this, I think, everyone would grant: that a man who is going to listen to philosophers needs a certain amount of practice in listening. Is that not so? Then what am I to speak to you about? Show me. What are you able to hear about? About good and evil? Whose? A horse's?" "No." "An ox's?" "No." "What then? A man's?" "Yes." "Do we know, then, what a man is, what his nature is, what the idea of him is? Are our ears open at all on this subject? Do you understand what nature is, or can you follow me at all when I speak? Shall I use proof with you? Do you understand even this, what a proof is? Do you know what is true and what is false? Am I to move you toward philosophy? Show me, then, what I will accomplish by talking with you. Stir up some eagerness in me. The right grass, when a sheep sees it, stirs its eagerness to eat, but if you set a stone or a loaf beside it, it will not be stirred. In the same way there are in us certain natural urges to speak too, when the one who will listen appears to be somebody, when he himself provokes us. But if he sits there like a stone or a bundle of fodder, how can he stir any desire in a man?" "So you will say nothing to me?" "I have only this to say to you. The man who does not know who he is, and what he was born for, and what sort of universe this is that he is in, and with what companions, and what things are good and evil, fine and shameful; who cannot follow an argument or a proof, or what is true and what is false, and cannot tell them apart: that man will not desire in keeping with nature, or avoid, or feel an impulse to act, or form a purpose; he will not assent, he will not refuse, he will not suspend judgment. In short, he will go about deaf and blind, thinking he is somebody when he is nobody. Is this the first time it has been so? Has it not been so ever since the human race began, that every error and every misfortune has come from this ignorance? This is all I have to say to you, and not even this gladly." "Why?" "Because you have not provoked me. What am I to look at in you that would stir me, as men who know horses are stirred by a horse of good breeding? Your body? You shape it shamefully. Your clothes? Those are soft too. Your bearing, your look? Nothing. When you want to hear a philosopher, do not say to him, 'You say nothing to me.' Only show yourself fit to listen, and you will see how you move the speaker."

LXXXII. So now, when you see friends, or brothers, who seem to be of one mind, do not pronounce on their friendship right away, not even if they swear to it, not even if they say they cannot be parted from each other. The ruling faculty of a bad man is not to be trusted; it is unstable, it has no judgment, it is overcome now by one impression and now by another. Do not ask what other people ask, whether they are born of the same parents and were brought up together and under the same slave who minded them, but this only: where do they place their interest, outside themselves or in the will? If outside, do not call them friends, any more than trustworthy, or steady, or courageous, or free; do not even call them human beings, if you have any sense. But if you hear that these men truly think the good lies only where the will is, where the right use of impressions is, do not trouble yourself any further about whether they are son and father, or brothers, or have gone to school together for a long time and are companions. Knowing this one thing, declare with confidence that they are friends, just as you would that they are trustworthy and just. For where else is friendship but where there is good faith, where there is self-respect, where there is a giving of what is noble and of nothing else?
LXXXIII. No one can rob us of our free will; no one can be its tyrant.

divergences.older: "Thou and I are of one mind. I am Thine" (Crossley)
divergences.lectio: "I am of one mind with you; I am yours."
divergences.note: The Perseus file of Schenkl prints ἴσος εἰμι, "I am your equal", which is what the manuscript has; σός, "yours", is the old correction that Crossley and most editors follow, and Lectio follows it too. "Your equal" would be a boast in the middle of a prayer of surrender.

divergences.phrase: ἐκεῖνον ἐπικαλοῦ βοηθὸν καὶ παραστάτην ὡς τοὺς Διοσκόρους ἐν χειμῶνι οἱ πλέοντες
divergences.older: "call upon Him to aid thee, like a comrade that stands beside thee in the fight" (Crossley)
divergences.lectio: "Call on him to help you and stand beside you, as sailors call on the Dioscuri in a storm."
divergences.note: Crossley stopped in mid-sentence and made a soldier's image out of παραστάτης. Epictetus's comparison is the sailors' prayer to Castor and Pollux, and the storm is the storm of impressions he has been describing. The sentence is given whole.

divergences.older: Crossley abridges Discourses II.24 heavily, marking four gaps with dots and making others silently
divergences.lectio: the same sentences, each given whole, with no dots
divergences.note: The concordance in SOURCES.md lists every piece. Left out, as in Crossley: the musician, the vine and the playful children, and the long example of Agamemnon and Achilles. "Are our ears open" is literally "are our ears bored through" (τετρημένα).
